claims.claim: Mare bishop of Amida, exiled at Petra, sent his deacon and notary Stephen to the royal city; God 'directed the virtuous Stephen to Theodora who came from the brothel (πορνεῖον), who was at that time a patrician, but eventually became queen also with King Justinian'; she made entreaty 'even with tears' to Justinian her husband, the king's nephew, to inform his uncle; an order went out for them to come to Alexandria
claims.witness: John of Ephesus, Lives of the Eastern Saints, tr. Brooks (combined file l.10440-10475; PO17 file l.10990-11005); a witness of the party she sheltered

claims.claim: Brooks dates Mare's expulsion probably to 521, and notes that Justinian's marriage followed a law dated 520-524
claims.witness: Brooks's notes (PO17 l.11012-11016)

claims.claim: John of Ephesus 'was a Monophysite' and his party 'refused to receive the council of Chalcedon'
claims.witness: R. Payne Smith's preface (john-of-ephesus EH l.286-291)

claims.claim: Her father Acacius, of the Green faction at Byzantium, was keeper of the wild beasts, 'called the Bear-keeper'; her mother sent the daughters on the stage; the rest is told as scandal
claims.witness: Procopius, Secret History IX (l.1829-1870); a hostile, private polemic

claims.claim: Dewing on the Secret History's account of her early years: 'both shocking and disgusting, but which, happily, we are not forced to regard as true'
claims.witness: Dewing's introduction to the Wars (wars-1-2 l.155-158)

claims.claim: Theodora was from Daman, a town above Callinicus; her father was a priest; she grew up 'dans la chasteté et la foi orthodoxe'; Justinian, sent as general, asked her parents for her; elsewhere Michael has Justinian take her as wife at Mabboug, the daughter of an orthodox priest, on an oath not to force the Synod on her
claims.witness: Michael the Syrian, Chronicle, tr. Chabot (tome 2 l.32343-32398, 13518-13522); twelfth century, from the anti-Chalcedonian side

claims.claim: Chabot: 'Ce récit paraît inventé par les Monophysites. Selon Evagrius et Niceph. Call., Theodora était originaire de Chypre'
claims.witness: Chabot's note 5 (tome 2 l.13545-13547); the held Evagrius, English (Walford) and Greek (Bidez-Parmentier), has no Cyprus line

claims.claim: In the Nika revolt the emperor and his court deliberated whether to flee in the ships; the Empress Theodora spoke, ending 'I approve a certain ancient saying that royalty is a good burial-shroud'
claims.witness: Procopius, Wars I.xxiv (wars-1-2 l.3102-3122). The speech is Procopius's composition, not her own recorded words (coordinator ruling 2026-11-14); Dewing notes his sounding phrases in speeches (l.196-199)

claims.claim: The Nika insurrection was in 532
claims.witness: Dewing's introduction (wars-1-2 l.131-132)

claims.claim: Justinian upheld Chalcedon and Theodora 'those who maintained the single nature: either because such were their real sentiments ... or by mutual understanding'; 'Our people she treated with the warmest kindness'; 'She also persuades Justinian to send for Severus'
claims.witness: Evagrius IV.10, tr. Walford (l.8149-8167); a later Chalcedonian historian

claims.claim: Their disagreement 'was seen to have been purposely arranged between them'; 'they split up the Christians into two parties'
claims.witness: Procopius, Secret History X (l.2069-2076); hostile

claims.claim: The king received Severus at Constantinople, 'disposed and incited thereto by Theodora the queen, who was devoted to Severus'
claims.witness: Syriac chronicle printed as Zachariah's, book IX ch. XIX (zachariah-rhetor l.13161-13169). Brooks: Zachariah's own work ended in 491 and the compiler followed him in books 3-6 only (l.300-314); so this is the compiler's, not Zachariah's

claims.claim: When she saw the king's wrath against Anthimus, who had laid his pall on the altar and departed, she hid him in a chamber in her palace, known only to her and two chamberlains, until the time of her death
claims.witness: John of Ephesus, Lives, tr. Brooks (combined l.25960-26003)

claims.claim: Length of Anthimus's hiding: about ten years in the Lives; Brooks notes she lived 12 years after his deprivation, and the Church History says 7
claims.witness: John of Ephesus, Lives (l.26001); Brooks's note (l.26025-26026)

claims.claim: She gathered in the palace of Hormisdas a community of persecuted men 'who did not fall short of the number of five hundred'; she made cells for them; 'would regularly once in every two or three days come down to them to be blessed by them'; even after her death 'she laid an injunction upon the king about it, and it was preserved'
claims.witness: John of Ephesus, Lives ch. 47 (combined l.25497-25655)

claims.claim: In the sixteenth year of Justinian's reign, at the request of 'Hereth Bar Gabala, the great king of the Saracens', she gave orders and James and Theodore were instituted, Theodore for Hirtha of the Saracens and James for Edessa
claims.witness: John of Ephesus, Lives ch. 50 (combined l.26697-26732)

claims.claim: She died in the twentieth year of Justinian, the year 859 of the Greeks
claims.witness: Michael the Syrian, tr. Chabot (tome 2 l.18175-18177); also quoted from Michael's Arabic in a note of Hamilton and Brooks (zachariah-rhetor l.15920-15925)

claims.claim: Her death in 548
claims.witness: Brooks's introduction to the Lives (combined l.248-249); an editor's year

claims.claim: 'the Christ-loving Theodora, who was perhaps appointed queen by God to be a support for the persecuted against the cruelty of the times'
claims.witness: John of Ephesus, Lives (combined l.17536-17538; OCR 'Fheodora', 'à support', 'eruelty')

claims.claim: Justinian honoured Cyprus for the glory of his wife Theodora, 'Κύπρον λαχούσης πατρίδα', whose homeland was Cyprus; and again 'εἰς τιμὴν τῆς γαμετῆς Θεοδώρας ... ἐκεῖθεν γὰρ ὥρμητο' (Latin 'conjugis suae Theodorae Augustae inde ortae')
claims.witness: Nicephorus Callistus, Ecclesiastical History, PG 147 (l.9790-9791, 14762-14765; Latin l.14727); a later Greek church historian

claims.claim: Justinian's reign began in 527
claims.witness: Dewing's introduction to the Wars (wars-1-2 l.68-69, 78-80); an editor's year

contested_claims.sides: Procopius, Secret History IX: daughter of Acacius the bear-keeper at Byzantium, on the stage and in a brothel as a girl (hostile; Dewing: 'we are not forced to regard as true'). John of Ephesus, of the party she sheltered: 'Theodora who came from the brothel'. Michael the Syrian (12th c.): a priest's daughter from Daman near Callinicus, raised in chastity. Chabot, on the Mabboug version: the story seems invented by the Monophysites; Evagrius and Nicephorus Callistus make her a native of Cyprus (not found in the held Walford Evagrius). Nicephorus Callistus (PG 147 l.9790-9791, 14762-14765): Cyprus was her homeland.

contested_claims.claim: Why Justinian and Theodora backed opposite sides on Chalcedon
contested_claims.sides: Evagrius IV.10: either real conviction or a mutual understanding; he does not decide. Procopius, Secret History X: a disagreement purposely arranged to divide their subjects (hostile).

John of Ephesus, Lives (combined l.26000-26002): ten years, until her death. John's Church History, as Brooks reports it (l.26024-26025): seven years. Brooks: she lived twelve years after his deprivation.

absent_details.note: The era 3 scan's 'c.497' rests on no held line. No held source gives a birth year.

No letter or writing of hers is held. The Nika speech is Procopius's composition. Mark's named ruling 'Theodora: Who' (era 3 scan, 2026-11-11), confirmed by the coordinator 2026-11-14, makes her a Who without them.

absent_details.detail: The scan's citation of 'Zachariah' for her death
absent_details.note: The death line at zachariah-rhetor l.15923 is a note quoting Michael the Syrian's Arabic, not the chronicle; and the chronicle's book IX is the compiler's, not Zachariah's (Brooks l.300-314).

claims.claim: On the Lord's day, at the order of Anastasius, Marinus and Plato in the church pulpit added to the hymn of the Trinity 'deipassianorum quaternitas'; many orthodox singing the old words and shouting down the 'perfidos praecones' were cut down in the church and died in prison
claims.witness: Marcellinus, Chronicle, year of the consuls Paulus and Moschianus (Mommsen l.8299-8306)

claims.claim: The next day a greater slaughter in the atrium of St Theodore; the crowds met in the forum of Constantine, cried for Areobindus as emperor, threw down Anastasius's images and statues; on the third day Anastasius sent them home 'solitis periuriis simulatisque vocibus, sese facturum cuncta promittens' and 'sine ullo rerum effectu'
claims.witness: Marcellinus (Mommsen l.8306-8355); a partisan account by a writer hostile to the change

claims.claim: The year of the hymn riot is 512
claims.witness: Mommsen's year heading (l.8299); an editor's date

claims.claim: 'ego vero vir clarissimus Marcellinus comes ... Orientale tantum secutus imperium' carried on Eusebius and Jerome from the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius (379) to 518, then added sixteen years to Justinian's fourth consulship (534); 'meum rusticum opus'
claims.witness: Marcellinus's preface (Mommsen l.4703-4720)

claims.claim: Cassiodorus: 'Marcellinus Illyricianus, qui adhuc patricii Iustiniani fertur egisse cancellos', who carried his work 'usque ad fores imperii triumphalis Augusti Iustiniani'; named after Eusebius and Jerome among the chroniclers; also four books on Constantinople and Jerusalem
claims.witness: Cassiodorus, Institutions I.17 and 25, quoted in Mommsen's preface (l.3049-3061, 3093-3098); also in Migne PL70 (l.83209-83228, 83696-83699)

claims.claim: Latin was his native language; he wrote at Constantinople
claims.witness: Mommsen's preface (l.3100-3104, 3162)

claims.claim: He became a cleric after leaving public service, before 527, reading Cassiodorus's 'meliore condicione devotus'
claims.witness: Mommsen's preface (l.3169-3172), Mommsen's inference

claims.claim: 'orthodoxum odium quaevis pagina apud Marcellinum spirat cum adversus haereticos omnes tum maxime adversus Nestorianos'; the author's zeal for Justinian
claims.witness: Mommsen's preface (l.3173-3175, 3184-3186)

claims.claim: The first edition ended at 518 and was issued under Justin, before 527; the second ran to 534
claims.witness: Marcellinus's preface; Mommsen's dating of the first edition (l.3176-3184)

claims.claim: The continuation 534-548, found in one of the two archetypes from which the manuscripts descend, and breaking off in 548, is not by Marcellinus: Cassiodorus does not know it and the preface does not mention it; probably written in the East
claims.witness: Mommsen's preface (l.3187-3194, 3717-3721)

claims.claim: The men who kept the old words were struck down in the church and, led off to prison, died there ('in eiusdem ecclesiae gremio caesi sunt ductique in carceres perierunt')
claims.witness: Marcellinus (Mommsen l.8305-8306)

absent_details.note: No held source gives them. Mommsen says his birth was not splendid, from Cassiodorus's notice of his post (l.3110-3111); this stays off the brief.

absent_details.detail: The four books on Constantinople and Jerusalem
absent_details.note: Named by Cassiodorus (Institutions I.25); not held.

claims.claim: Sailing for Further India and almost across to Barbaria, near the mouth of the ocean, he saw a great flight of the birds called Souspha; all were in alarm, and the men of experience called out to the pilot: 'Steer the ship to port and make for the gulf, or we shall be swept along by the currents and be carried into the ocean and be lost.'
claims.witness: Cosmas, Book II, tr. McCrindle (cosmas mccrindle1897 l.3289-3340)

claims.claim: Made voyages for commercial purposes in three gulfs, the Roman, the Arabian and the Persian
claims.witness: Cosmas, Book II (l.3281-3283)

claims.claim: Most probably a native of Alexandria; a merchant in his earlier life; later retired to a cloister
claims.witness: McCrindle's introduction (l.578-586, 736-741); McCrindle's inference

claims.claim: Surnamed Indicopleustes, or the Indian Navigator
claims.witness: McCrindle's introduction (l.443-445)

claims.claim: Whether he reached India: Cosmas does not say whether the voyage got there; McCrindle holds that Book XI shows personal knowledge; Freese says it is doubtful whether he deserves the title
claims.witness: McCrindle (l.626-638); Freese's note to Photius cod. 36 (photius freese1920 l.2605-2607)

claims.claim: Whether 'Cosmas' was his own name: Voss and Fabricius held he was named for his work on the kosmos; McCrindle: 'this must remain an open question'
claims.witness: McCrindle (l.563-574)

claims.claim: At Adulis some five and twenty years before, at the beginning of Justin's reign, while Elesbaan, king of the Axomites, prepared an expedition against the Homerites, the governor asked him and the merchant Menas, later a monk at Rhaithu, to copy the inscriptions on the Chair and the tablet
claims.witness: Cosmas, Book II (l.4069-4112)

claims.claim: The visit was in 525 and the writing about 547; Book X was written in the year before 536
claims.witness: McCrindle (l.695-698, 839-862); McCrindle's reckoning, with Salt's dates (l.4117-4119)

claims.claim: He explained the tabernacle as 'a type and copy of the whole world', learned from the divine scriptures and 'from the living voice of that most divine man and great teacher Patricius', who set out from Chaldaea with his disciple Thomas of Edessa and was appointed 'Bishop Catholic' of Persia
claims.witness: Cosmas, Book II (l.2526-2545)

claims.claim: Patricius 'was a Magian and was called by the Syrians Abas or Mar-Abas'; Montfaucon's Latin makes Patricius die at Byzantium and Thomas become Primate, which McCrindle rejects
claims.witness: McCrindle's note (l.2557-2563)

claims.claim: Most probably a Nestorian, by De La Croze's arguments and one of McCrindle's own; against this he calls Mary the Mother of God, 'an expression abhorrent to the Nestorians'
claims.witness: McCrindle (l.781-832)

claims.claim: Photius: neither sky nor earth is spherical; the sky is a vault and the earth a rectangular plane; the style poor; 'he may fairly be regarded as a fabulist rather than a trustworthy authority'
claims.witness: Photius, Library cod. 36, tr. Freese (l.2591-2641)

claims.claim: In Taprobane 'there is a Church of Christians, with clergy and a body of believers'; in Male, where the pepper grows, a church; at Calliana 'a bishop, who is appointed from Persia'; on the island of Dioscorides clergy ordained in Persia; churches with bishops throughout Persia
'This I avouch to be the veritable fact, from what I have seen and heard in the many places which I have visited.'
claims.witness: Cosmas, Book III (l.7187-7189)

claims.claim: Photius's verdict 'has not been endorsed by modern opinion'
claims.witness: McCrindle (l.886-888)

claims.claim: Cosmas wrote his Topography about 547, his voyages falling between 520 and 525; his account gives 'des renseignements précieux sur l'extension de l'Église de Perse à cette époque'
claims.witness: Labourt (labourt_le-christianisme-dans-l-empire-perse-sassanide-fra_1904.txt l.9618-9622)

claims.claim: Card tradition: the census lists him among the people of Aksumite Christianity (year 522); the corpus map files his whole work under the Church of the East as context, 'Provisional on his affiliation'
claims.witness: cic-website/data/world-census.json, aksumite-christianity people; cic/corpus-map/the-church-of-the-east-under-persia.yaml l.113-123

contested_claims.claim: Whether Cosmas belonged to the Church of the East
contested_claims.sides: De La Croze, followed by McCrindle: most probably (l.781-810). McCrindle himself notes the passage calling Mary the Mother of God, against it (l.811-832). Photius and Montfaucon do not raise it (l.786-788).
McCrindle: Book XI shows personal knowledge (l.629-636). Freese: doubtful whether he deserves the title Indian Navigator (photius l.2605-2607).

absent_details.note: No held source names them. McCrindle says the Topography is the source for his life; the Library holds no other account of his life.
McCrindle says only the Topography survives of his works on geography, cosmography and Scripture (l.741-743); Photius reports a commentary on the Song of Songs (l.2645-2647).

claims.claim: The questions are headed as Dorotheus's 'Ad magnum senem sanctum Barsanuphium, et ad ejus discipulum abbatem Joannem, cognomento Prophetam, ob perspicaciae donum quod habuit a Deo'; Interrogatio I is headed 'Abbatis Dorothei ad abbatem Joannem'
claims.witness: Migne, PG 88 (dorotheus-gaza migne-pg88 l.139571-139581)

claims.claim: Q1: how can I restrain too great freedom and govern my tongue? A: 'Per luctum.' Q2: how can I keep mourning while dealing daily with people of the world? A: 'Non fletus per lacrymas, sed per fletum lacrymae'
claims.witness: Interrogatio 1 and 2, Latin of PG 88 (l.139588-139589, 139700-139714)

claims.claim: No later question or answer in the set is marked by speaker
claims.witness: Read through PG 88 l.139581-142030; only the first heading names John

claims.claim: Dorotheus had as master the abbot John, 'illustrem Barsanuphii discipulum et Prophetae titulo clarum'; the disciple who wrote the Life of Saint Dositheus says Dorotheus knew the two great old men when he withdrew to the coenobium of the abbot Seridus
claims.witness: Migne's Notitia on Dorotheus (l.121957-121961)

claims.claim: Migne heads the notice 'ANNO DOMINI DXCVI'; the Bollandists, Fabricius and Cave place Dorotheus at the end of the sixth century; the year of his death is not known

Dorotheus took everything to the abbot John; when his thought said 'Quid nunc turbare senem pergas? hoc tibi dicturus est quod ego', he answered 'Anathema tibi' and went to the father, and often the old man answered just as the thought had foreseen
claims.witness: Dorotheus, Doctrina, PG 88 (l.127966-127978)

claims.claim: Feeling no tribulation though Scripture speaks of many, he asked the abbot John, disciple of Barsanuphius, by letter; the old man answered that whoever gives himself to the obedience of the fathers gains this rest and security from God
claims.witness: Dorotheus, Doctrina I, PG 88 (l.124095-124108, 128013-128017); Benedict of Aniane reports the same from Dorotheus (benedict-aniane pl103 l.69675-69688)

claims.claim: The successive heads of the monastery were Barsanuphius, Seridus and Dorotheus; Seridus's monastery was at Thabatha, which Nau places towards Choubana, not far from the sea
claims.witness: Nau, appendix to the Plerophories (po08 l.11422-11500); Nau's reading

claims.claim: Thabatha is 'about five miles to the south of Gaza, a city of Palestine'
claims.witness: Jerome, Life of Hilarion, NPNF 2.6 (npnf206 l.30129-30130)

claims.claim: There were two Dorotheuses and two Barsanuphiuses, one pair defending the errors of Severus, the other holding sound doctrine; Theodore the Studite is cited as witness
claims.witness: Anonymous preface, Latin of PG 88 (l.122100-122119); Migne prints it as 'ANONYMI PRAEFATIO'

claims.claim: Theodore, answering the 'pernicious teaching of Pamphilus who came from the East', separates the Barsanuphius, Isaiah and Dorotheus who led the Acephali and were anathematized by Sophronius from the holy men he accepts, and says 'Barsanuphii imago in Magna ecclesia juxta sanctos Patres Antonium, Ephraim aliosque rite dicata et collocata visitur'
claims.witness: Theodore the Studite, quoted in the anonymous preface (l.122119-122131, 122182-122207; Greek l.122160-122170)

claims.claim: Theodore the Studite numbers Barsanuphius and Dorotheus among the holy fathers whose lives and writings he receives
claims.witness: Migne's Notitia, quoting Theodore (l.121971-121978)

claims.claim: The Latin is Hilarion of Verona's version, revised by Fronto Ducaeus

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Barsanuphius of these answers is the one condemned with the Acephali
contested_claims.sides: The anonymous preface and Theodore the Studite: there were two of each name, and the condemned ones were others (l.122100-122131, 122182-122207). The 'Pamphilus from the East' whom Theodore answers attacked Barsanuphius, Isaiah and Dorotheus as Acephali (l.122127-122131). No held modern scholar was found discussing it.

absent_details.note: No held source gives them. The scan's 'first half of the sixth century' rests on no held line; Migne's year 596 is for Dorotheus.

Only Dorotheus's set of questions is held, in Latin. The census cites John Chryssavgis's English of about 850 letters, which is not held. The census line that Barsanuphius was an Egyptian walled into a cell around 520 was not found in any held file.
No held line calls them 'of Gaza'. The place rests on Nau's placing of Seridus's monastery near Thabatha and on Jerome's placing of Thabatha south of Gaza.

claims.claim: Mar Aba, patriarch, and his bishops went into the land of Kashkar; at the town of Zizwarda all the people of Kashkar agreed and chose Mar Samuel as bishop; the two rival bishops of the time of discord were stripped of every episcopal title and submitted 'avec grande joie' to Samuel, serving as priests
claims.witness: Synod of Mar Aba, tr. Chabot (synodicon-orientale chabot1902 l.21159-21180)

claims.claim: The synod's record opens by saying that the duality of the patriarchate introduced by Mar Elisha and Mar Narses had wholly ceased and the single patriarchal rule of Seleucia-Ctesiphon was restored
claims.witness: Synod of Mar Aba, tr. Chabot (l.20909-20923, 21014-21016)

claims.claim: The first document is dated in the month Shahrir of the 13th year of Kosrau and the 5th year of Aba's patriarchate; Chabot reckons December 543 to January 544 and concludes he was elected in January 540
claims.witness: Chabot's heading [A.D. 544] and note (l.20903-20915, 20945-20953, 20979-20980); Chabot's reckoning

claims.claim: The documents under the title 'Synod of Mar Aba' were six; the first, fourth and fifth are in the manuscripts here, Chabot adds the third, and puts fragments of the second and sixth in appendices
claims.witness: Chabot's note (l.21137-21142)

claims.claim: A longer History of Mar Aba, edited by Bedjan (1895) and held in Braun's German,, 'aurait besoin d'un examen critique minutieux' and lacks chronological data; Chabot's outline: born a Zoroastrian, baptized at Hira, studied at Nisibis, learned Greek at Edessa from his disciple Thomas, journeyed to Constantinople, taught at Nisibis, elected January 540, founded a school at Seleucia, worked to restore peace and discipline after the schism of Narses and Elisha, was persecuted after controversies with the magi, spent several years in prison and was exiled to Adherbaidjan
claims.witness: Chabot's note (l.20963-20995); the Bedjan Life is not held

claims.claim: According to the author of his Life he regained the king's favour and died in peace on his see; according to Bar Hebraeus, having returned to Seleucia against the king's ban, he was imprisoned and died there; death on the second Friday of Lent (per the Life), in 552 (per the acts of the synod of Mar Joseph); the Nestorians honour him as a saint

Mar Abba the Great had been a magus, most tenacious of his religion; refusing the scholar Joseph a place in his boat on the Tigris, he was held back by winds each time until he took him aboard; Joseph showed him he was a Christian and taught him
claims.witness: Mari ibn Sulayman, tr. Gismondi (mari gismondi1899 l.14092-14100, 14003-14006); a twelfth-century account told as a wonder

claims.claim: Baptized, he went to Nisibis to learn sacred doctrine, then into Roman territory, a hearer of Thomas of Edessa, from whom he learned Greek; the two went to Constantinople, refused to anathematize 'tres illos patres', were nearly killed and fled to Nisibis, where he taught; after the death of Paul he was given the primacy; he founded a school at Madain
claims.witness: Mari, tr. Gismondi (l.14006-14016)

claims.claim: The magi envied him because he was of their race and had changed their customs and allowed each man only one wife; with Anushirvan's favour he was held seven years in prison in Adorbigan, not ceasing to care for his flock; he told the king, 'si meam vis necem occide me' (OCR 'nocem occido')
claims.witness: Mari, tr. Gismondi (l.14016-14025)

claims.claim: In the time of Narses and Elisha each ordained a bishop in every region, so that two altars rose in every church
claims.witness: Mari, tr. Gismondi (l.14049-14052)

claims.claim: Grieving over the afflictions of clergy and churches, he died of an illness after some days, on a Friday, the third day of Lent; his disciple Qyura carried him to Hira and built a monastery over the tomb; he led the church sixteen years; his disciples included the patriarch Ezekiel and Thomas of Edessa
claims.witness: Mari, tr. Gismondi (l.13990-14000)

claims.claim: A school he built on the site of a fire temple stood until the patriarch Ezekiel restored it
claims.witness: Mari, tr. Gismondi (l.13955-13977), told with a fire-walking wonder

claims.claim: Abas, once a magus, was baptized and went to Nisibis; at Edessa his Greek teacher was Thomas, a Jacobite, with whom he went to Alexandria; expelled from Seleucia he stayed in Adorbigana, returned to Seleucia thinking himself forgotten, was chained by the king and died in prison
claims.witness: Bar Hebraeus, Chronicon ecclesiasticum, tr. Abbeloos and Lamy (barhebraeus vol3 l.5226-5240, 5512-5525); a hostile West Syriac witness of the 1200s

claims.claim: Sat from 538 to 552
claims.witness: Abbeloos and Lamy's note to Bar Hebraeus (vol3 l.5254)

claims.claim: God established marriage 'comme un lien d'amour de l'union chaste et légitime de l'homme et de la femme'; the letter forbids taking a second wife while the first lives and marriage to a father's wife and other close kin 'comme les mages'
claims.witness: Letter of Mar Aba on the rule of the faithful, tr. Chabot (l.22100-22101, 22273-22297; OCR 'Funion', 'Fhomme')

claims.claim: Patricius, Cosmas's teacher, who became Bishop Catholic of all Persia, 'was a Magian and was called by the Syrians Abas or Mar-Abas'
claims.witness: McCrindle's note to Cosmas Book II (cosmas mccrindle1897 l.2557-2563); McCrindle's identification

claims.claim: The Life: Mar Aba was at first a pagan, learned in Persian letters; notables of his district drew him into state service and made him Arzabed
claims.witness: Life of Mar Aba, tr. Braun (persian-martyr-acts braun1915 l.10670-10678); Labourt: born to a Mazdean family, in the administrative career (labourt1904 l.9483-9492)

claims.claim: The Life: he was baptized in the village of 'KD (Labourt: Akda)
claims.witness: Life, tr. Braun (persian-martyr-acts braun1915 l.10826); Labourt l.9556, 'Au bourg d''Akda, d'après sa Vie, p. 211; à Hira, d'après MARE, p. 44'

claims.claim: The Life: he studied at the school of Nisibis, went to Edessa, where Thomas taught him Greek, and later taught
claims.witness: Life, tr. Braun (persian-martyr-acts braun1915 l.10833-10885); Labourt quoting the Life, 'il passa un certain temps dans l'enseignement' (l.9816-9818)

claims.claim: The Life: he came back to his see after nine years of struggle
claims.witness: Life, tr. Braun (persian-martyr-acts braun1915 l.12234-12240)

claims.claim: The Life: he lived beside the church of Bet Narkos; ill after his long imprisonment, he died on the Friday of the second week of Lent; doctors the king sent could not heal him
claims.witness: Life, tr. Braun (persian-martyr-acts braun1915 l.12290, 12318-12322)

claims.claim: The Life: after seven days in the cathedral of Koke his body was carried with honour to the monastery of Seleucia; Braun notes that Mari has him buried at Hira by his disciple
claims.witness: Life, tr. Braun (persian-martyr-acts braun1915 l.12329-12355, note l.12361-12362)

claims.claim: He died on 29 February 552 at Seleucia, near the church of Beit Narqos; later chroniclers may set his death at Hira because of the Arab king's retinue
The author of the Life was really, as he claims, a disciple of the catholicos
claims.witness: Labourt (l.9559-9562)

claims.claim: The existence of the school of Seleucia at this time seems problematic
claims.witness: Labourt (l.9843-9844)

contested_claims.sides: The Life, held in Braun's German (l.12318-12322), and as Chabot reports it: he regained the king's favour and died in peace on his see (l.20994-20995). Bar Hebraeus: returned to Seleucia against the king's ban, chained and died in prison (vol3 l.5519-5525; reported by Chabot l.20995-20998, 20929-20931). Mari ibn Sulayman: died of an illness after some days, grieving (l.13991-13997).
Chabot: January 540, from the synod's dating (l.20945-20953, 20979). Abbeloos and Lamy: 538 (vol3 l.5254). Mari's sixteen years of rule (l.13999) fit neither with 552.

The Life: the village of 'KD, Akda in Labourt's reading (Braun l.10826; Labourt l.9556). Mari ibn Sulayman: Hira (Labourt l.9556, citing Mari p. 44); Chabot's outline follows Hira (Chabot l.20963-20979).

The Life: the monastery of Seleucia (Braun l.12350-12355; Labourt l.10985-10987). Mari ibn Sulayman: at Hira, by his disciple Qyura, under a monastery (Gismondi l.13997-13999; Braun's note l.12361-12362).

absent_details.note: The Syriac of Paul Bedjan's edition is not held; the Life is held in Braun's German (l.10660-12360) and retold by Labourt (l.9479-11010). Richard Payne's English, which the census entry cites, was not checked.
No held source gives it. Labourt gives his home on the Tigris opposite Hale, in the district of Radan, and his Mazdean family (l.9483-9488).

claims.claim: Theodora sent Anthemius the scribe to Rome; he found Vigilius in the church of Saint Cecilia on 22 November, her feast, while he was distributing gifts, took him to the Tiber and set him on a ship; the people threw stones and sticks and cried 'Your hunger go with you!'
claims.witness: Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11699-11721)

claims.claim: The Romans accuse Vigilius of murder ('We declare him to be a murderer')
claims.witness: Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11655-11660); the Book of the Popes' report; Loomis calls this part of the book often partisan (l.575-576). The same life has Vigilius refuse Theodora (l.11646-11651)

claims.claim: The life of Vigilius in the Book of the Popes is full of inaccuracies and mistakes; Duchesne argues its author wrote no earlier than the time of Pelagius II
claims.witness: Loomis's note, citing Duchesne (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11536-11546); Pelagius II's dates 579-590 from Loomis's contents (l.474)

claims.claim: The circumstances of his departure from Rome are described nowhere else; Facundus alone adds that all Rome drove him out
claims.witness: Loomis's note (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11734-11738)

claims.claim: Vigilius left Rome in 544 or 545
claims.witness: Loomis's note, citing Duchesne and Jaffé (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11743-11746)

claims.claim: Vigilius was a Roman, son of John the consul, and a deacon who had been delegate to Constantinople
claims.witness: Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11524, 11314)

claims.claim: A suspicion arose that Silverius was dealing treasonably with the Goths; Belisarius sent him to Greece and 'a little later appointed another man, Vigilius by name, to the office of chief priest'
claims.witness: Procopius, Wars V.xxv, tr. Dewing (procopius_wars-5-6-gothic_dewing1919.txt l.3473-3477)

claims.claim: In 537 Belisarius removed Silverius and ordained the deacon Vigilius in his place
claims.witness: Continuation of Marcellinus's chronicle, year 537 (chronica-minora-2 (Mommsen 1894) l.8959-8961)

claims.claim: Theodora had Vigilius promise in secret that as pope he would annul Chalcedon and approve the faith of Theodosius, Anthemius and Severus, and offered an order to Belisarius and seven hundred thousand sesterces
claims.witness: Liberatus, Breviarium 22 (PL 68, liberatus-victor-tunnunensis-primasius-junillus-pl68-lat_migne1866.txt l.81553-81640), as quoted in English by Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11389-11400); hostile to Vigilius by Mommsen's judgment (chronica-minora-2 l.17574-17578) and by the PL 68 editor's note that Liberatus tells it to cast odium on Vigilius (l.81654-81657)

claims.claim: Theodora drew from Vigilius, before his ordination, a secret written pledge to condemn the Three Chapters; Antonina compelled him to write to Theodosius, Anthimus and Severus as Catholics; Victor copies the letter
claims.witness: Victor of Tunnuna, year 542 (chronica-minora-2 (Mommsen 1894) l.18888-18910)

claims.claim: Liberatus and Victor, of the same party and stern defenders of Chalcedon, embittered 'iusto odio' against Vigilius, 'perhaps the worst' of bad popes, both bring forward the letter to the Eastern bishops, whether truly his or, as others think, forged; it was certainly published at the time and eagerly received
claims.witness: Mommsen's introduction to Victor (chronica-minora-2 (Mommsen 1894) l.17574-17582)

claims.claim: Unless Vigilius was an absolutely unscrupulous double-dealer, the letter to Anthemius must be classed as a forgery
claims.witness: Loomis's note, citing Duchesne (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11667-11690)

claims.claim: The Three Chapters were the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret's writings against Cyril, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa to Maris
claims.witness: Bossuet, as printed by Percival (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.22886-22889); Theodoret 'Cyri episcopi' in Victor (chronica-minora-2 (Mommsen 1894) l.18898)

claims.claim: In 548 Vigilius issued the Judicatum, anathematizing the Three Chapters but maintaining his adherence to Chalcedon
claims.witness: Loomis's note (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11787-11791); 11 April 548 in Bossuet's account as printed by Percival (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.22951-22953)

claims.claim: In 550 the African bishops cut Vigilius off from Catholic communion, leaving him a place for repentance
claims.witness: Victor of Tunnuna, year 550 (chronica-minora-2 (Mommsen 1894) l.19047-19049); also Bossuet in Percival (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.22955-22958)

claims.claim: The council opened on 5 May 553 by the emperor's command, without the pope's assent
claims.witness: Hefele, as printed by Percival (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.22877-22878)

claims.claim: The Constitutum is dated 'prid. Iduum Maiarum', in Justinian's 27th year, at Constantinople: 14 May 553
claims.witness: Avellana ep. 83, ed. Guenther (collectio-avellana_..._v1-lat_guenther1895.txt l.24223-24225; Guenther's date l.18303)

claims.claim: Of Theodore of Mopsuestia: 'eum nostra non audemus condemnare sententia sed nec ab alio quoquam condemnari concedimus'
claims.witness: Constitutum (Avellana v1, l.22362-22363)

claims.claim: The council, after the Constitutum, condemned the Three Chapters and those who defended them
claims.witness: Bossuet, as printed by Percival (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.22976-22986); Percival's excursus (l.24497-24501)

claims.claim: Letter to Eutychius, dated 'VI. Id. Dec.', which Percival gives as A.D. 553: Vigilius condemns the Three Chapters and annuls whatever he or others said in their defence
claims.witness: Decretal letter, tr. Percival (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.24465-24478, 24490-24492)

claims.claim: Some doubted the decretal's genuineness (Harduin, after Garnerius), but the learned have generally accepted it as genuine
claims.witness: Percival's note (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.24339-24343)

claims.claim: 'there ought to be no shame when what was at first omitted is made public after it is discovered by a further study of the truth'; Augustine retracted and corrected some of his own writings
claims.witness: Decretal letter, tr. Percival (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.24385-24393)

claims.claim: He died at Syracuse in Sicily of the stone and was buried at Saint Marcellus on the Via Salaria
claims.witness: Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11916-11920)

claims.claim: A contemporary record gives his death as 7 June 555
claims.witness: Loomis's note, citing Duchesne (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11934-11937); the year 555 is the reckoning of the third indiction in Loomis's bracket from Duchesne

claims.claim: He died at the end of 554 or the beginning of 555
claims.witness: Percival (npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml l.24512-24513)

claims.claim: The account of his maltreatment at Constantinople is partly legendary
claims.witness: Loomis's note (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11834-11839)

claims.claim: The Three Chapters quarrel brought a new schism between East and West, which lasted seventy years
claims.witness: Loomis's note (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11796-11798)

claims.claim: Liberatus says Silverius was handed to Vigilius's guards and died of starvation on Palmaria; the guilt seems to rest partly on Antonina and partly on Vigilius
claims.witness: Liberatus as quoted by Loomis; Loomis's judgment (Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (liber-pontificalis_book-of-the-popes-v1_loomis1916.txt l.11477-11493)

claims.claim: The Book of the Popes' life of Silverius: Vigilius took Silverius 'as if in his own charge', sent him into exile to Pontiae and fed him with the bread of tribulation; he died a confessor
claims.witness: Book of the Popes, tr. Loomis (l.11443-11471); Loomis, after Duchesne, gives this part to a later biographer sympathetic to Silverius (l.11328-11338)

claims.claim: A chronicle note printed with Marcellinus puts his death in Sicily under 'Indictione II. XIII p. c. Basilii'
claims.witness: chronica-minora-2 (Mommsen 1894) l.3260-3263

contested_claims.sides: Procopius (Wars V.xxv, l.3473-3477): Belisarius appointed him after sending Silverius away, with no word of a bargain. Liberatus (Breviarium 22, via Loomis l.11389-11400) and Victor of Tunnuna (year 542, Mommsen l.18888-18902): Theodora won a secret promise from him first. Mommsen (l.17574-17578) calls Liberatus and Victor bitterly hostile to Vigilius.

contested_claims.claim: Whether Vigilius wrote the letter to Theodosius, Anthimus and Severus
contested_claims.sides: Liberatus and Victor copy it as his. Loomis, citing Duchesne (l.11683-11690): a forgery unless he was a shameless double-dealer. Mommsen (l.17578-17580): leaves it open, noting that others think it forged, and says it was published and received at the time.

contested_claims.claim: Whether the letter to Eutychius is genuine
contested_claims.sides: Harduin, after Garnerius: forged. Percival (l.24339-24343): the learned have generally accepted it.

A contemporary record cited by Duchesne, via Loomis (l.11934-11937): 'the seventh day before the Ides of June in the third indiction', which Duchesne's bracket gives as 7 June 555. Percival (l.24512-24513): the end of 554 or the start of 555. A chronicle note printed with Marcellinus (Mommsen l.3260-3263): the second indiction, thirteenth year after Basil's consulship.

contested_claims.claim: Vigilius's part in the death of Silverius
contested_claims.sides: Liberatus (Breviarium 22, PL 68 l.81613-81617, via Loomis l.11484-11488): Silverius was handed to Vigilius's guards and starved on Palmaria. The Book of the Popes' life of Silverius (Loomis l.11443-11471): Vigilius took him into his own charge and sent him into exile, where he died a confessor. Procopius's Secret History, as Loomis reports it (l.11488-11491): Antonina, wife of Belisarius, brought about his death. Loomis (l.11492-11493): the guilt rests partly on Antonina and partly on Vigilius.

absent_details.note: No source used here gives them.
Reported by Loomis and by Bossuet in Percival; its text is not in the sources used here.

claims.claim: On the feast of Christ's nativity the Mother of God appeared to Romanos in sleep and gave him a roll of paper, saying 'Accipe chartam et comede eam'; he seemed to swallow it, woke, went up the ambo and sang 'Virgo parit hodie supersubstantialem Filium'
claims.witness: Menologion notice, in Pitra's Latin (Pitra, romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.6811-6833); a saint's story

claims.claim: Pitra says the notice comes from the Menologion of the emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus (Vatican codex 1613); it is a very short eulogy, and almost nothing more is recorded of Romanos elsewhere
claims.witness: Pitra's note (romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.6791-6797); Pitra's attribution of the manuscript

claims.claim: Vatican codex 1613 is the Menologion of the emperor Basil
claims.witness: Migne, PG 99, 'Ex Menologio Basilii imperatoris. Cod. Vatic. n. 1613' (theodore-studite_opera-omnia-pg99-grc-lat_migne1860.txt l.7839); the Bollandists, 'Menologio Graecorum, jussu Basilii Porphyrogeniti Imperatoris' (acta-sanctorum_martii-tomus-3-lat-grc_palme1865.txt l.180301-180302); Assemani (assemani_bibliotheca-orientalis-tomus3-pars2-de-syris-nestorianis-lat_1728.txt l.39715-39716); 'the menologion of Basilius II (976-1025) in the Vatican Library' (studia-biblica-et-ecclesiastica-v5-life-of-st-nino_wardrop1903.txt l.16382-16386)

claims.claim: Constantine Porphyrogenitus reigned 944-959
claims.witness: Samuel H. Cross (russian-primary-chronicle_cross1930.txt l.6708)

claims.claim: Romanos came from Syria, was a deacon of the church of Berytus, came to Constantinople in the time of the emperor Anastasius, stayed at the church of the Mother of God in the quarter of Cyrus, kept vigil at Blachernae, wrote about a thousand kontakia for other feasts, and died
claims.witness: Menologion notice, in Pitra's Latin (Pitra, romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.6811-6833)

claims.claim: The roll in the dream gave the kontakion its name
claims.witness: Pitra's note 5 (Pitra, romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.6845-6849)

claims.claim: Whether the first or the second emperor Anastasius is meant is open; Pitra looks to the third poem for marks of time, sets out events of Anastasius I's reign (earthquakes of 494 and 503, the Persian war of 502-504) and of Anastasius II's (713-716), and says it is not at all clear whether Romanos flourished then
claims.witness: Pitra's notes (Pitra, romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.6808-6811 and the notes to Canticum III, l.8230-8250)

claims.claim: Pitra printed three poems, selected from many sent from the monastery of Saint John on Patmos, with Latin prose renderings: on Stephen the protomartyr, on Joseph the chaste, on the ten virgins
claims.witness: Pitra (Pitra, romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.6923, 6965-6973, 7399, 8079)

claims.claim: Acrostics, per Pitra's headings: 'Humilis Romani' (Stephen; ten virgins), 'Alphabetum Romani' (Joseph)
claims.witness: Pitra's headings (Pitra, romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.6926-6929, 7400, 8082)

claims.claim: The ten virgins refrain, in Pitra's Latin: 'Ne foris maneamus, clamantes: Aperi nobis!'
claims.witness: Pitra (Pitra, romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.8085-8086)

claims.claim: Pitra titles Romanos 'veterum melodorum princeps'
claims.witness: Pitra's title page (Pitra, romanos-melodist_cantica-grc_pitra1888.txt l.309)

claims.claim: The Greek of the kontakia is not recoverable from the scanned file; only Pitra's Latin and apparatus can be read
claims.witness: The Library file's own content note (l.27-36), checked: no Greek-script characters

claims.claim: A later Greek Synaxaristes, revised by Nikodemos the Hagiorite, gives Romanos's home city as Emesa, now Homs, makes him a deacon of Berytus who came to Constantinople in the time of the emperor Anastasius, and retells the dream, the ambo and the thousand kontakia
claims.witness: Synaxaristes, 1 October (nikodemos-hagiorite_synaxaristes-vol1-sep-feb-grc_1900.txt l.13987-14063); later than the Menologion and in the same tradition

contested_claims.sides: Pitra (l.6791): the Menologion of the emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus, Vatican 1613. Migne, PG 99 (l.7839), the Bollandists (Acta Sanctorum Martii III l.180301-180302), Assemani (l.39715-39716) and the Studia Biblica essay (l.16382-16386): the Menologion of the emperor Basil.

contested_claims.claim: Which emperor Anastasius the Menologion notice means, and so when Romanos lived
contested_claims.sides: Pitra (l.6808-6811, 8230-8250) asks whether Anastasius I or Anastasius II (713-716) is meant and sets out events of both reigns; he says it is not at all clear that Romanos flourished under the second. The Library file header's 'c. 490-c. 556' and the era 3 scan's dates rest on no held scholar's argument. Nikodemos's Synaxaristes (l.13998-13999) also places his coming under the emperor Anastasius; the year it gives is garbled in the OCR (read by the R1 reviewer as 496, under Anastasius I) and is not used.

absent_details.detail: His years of birth and death
absent_details.note: Neither the notice nor Pitra gives them. The scan's c.490-c.556 comes from the Library file header and is not used.
Printed in Pitra's volume but unreadable in the scanned copy; the brief quotes only Pitra's Latin.

absent_details.detail: A witness older than the Menologion notice
absent_details.note: Pitra says almost nothing more is recorded of him. Nikodemos's Synaxaristes (l.13987-14063) is later and follows the same tradition; its year for his coming to Constantinople is not legible in the OCR and is not used.

claims.claim: Anastasius son of Pamphilus, at the head of the duchy of Palestine, was sent to make John communicate with Severus and anathematize Chalcedon, or else remove him; released, the archbishop brought all the monks into the holy city by night, 'au dire de ceux qui ont compté cette multitude', ten thousand; on Sunday in the church of the protomartyr Stephen he mounted the ambo with Theodosius and Sabas; the people shouted for long hours 'Anathématise les hérétiques et confirme le concile'; the three anathematized Nestorius, Eutyches, Severus and Soterichus and whoever did not receive Chalcedon; the duke, fearing the monks, fled to Caesarea
claims.witness: Cyril, Life of Sabas, extract tr. Kugener (zacharias-scholasticus vie-de-severe-po2 kugener1903 l.25076-25079, 25095-25111, 25188-25206)

claims.claim: In his narration Cyril calls Severus 'le chef des Acéphales'
claims.witness: Life of Sabas extract, tr. Kugener (l.24740, 24821); a partisan Chalcedonian account

claims.claim: 'Cyrille né à Scythopolis en Galilée vers 523, et mourut après 557'; his Life of Sabas is 'une source du plus grand prix pour l'histoire de l'Église de Jérusalem et du monachisme palestinien'
claims.witness: Kugener's note (l.24697-24699; OCR 'Cyrille n rh a Scythopolis en Galilee')

claims.claim: He saw Euthymius's coffin continually flowing with miracles and wondered how he gained such confidence with God; he met many old men of the desert who had heard of Euthymius, some from Sabas, and wrote down what each told him
claims.witness: Cyril, Life of Euthymius, Latin tr. Cotelier (cyril-scythopolis cotelier1681 l.45445-45475; OCR rough)

claims.claim: He names the anchorite Cyriacus as his informant: 'Haec mihi Anachoreta Cyriacus narravit'
claims.witness: Life of Euthymius, Latin (l.31776-31777; OCR 'Hzc mihi')

claims.claim: Euthymius and Sabas appeared to him; Sabas said Cyril, Euthymius's son, held the paper but could not even begin; Euthymius drew a silver alabaster jar of honey from his breast, dipped a probe and put it in his mouth; on waking the sweetness remained in his mouth; so he began the present work and was eager to write the deeds of Sabas in another
claims.witness: Life of Euthymius, Latin (l.45586-45700)

claims.claim: He later lived in a laura the Origenists had held, by leave of the solitary John, a bishop
claims.witness: Life of Euthymius, Latin (l.45535-45552); OCR rough, read in part

claims.claim: The Life was first written by Cyril, monk of Scythopolis, 'clarissimo Vitarum scriptore' (OCR 'clariffimo V itarum feri- ptore'); Cotelier's copy lacks the opening letter cited elsewhere, though Allatius's quotations from Cyril's Life occur in it
claims.witness: Cotelier's notes (l.72939-72971)

absent_details.note: The scan's c.525-c.559 rests only on the Library's file header. Kugener gives about 523 to after 557; no other held source gives years.

absent_details.detail: The Life of Sabas and his other Lives
absent_details.note: Only Kugener's extracts on Severus from the Life of Sabas are held; the full Life of Sabas, in Cotelier's volume 3, is not, and no other Life by Cyril is held.
The held texts give his vision, his informants and the move to a laura; they give no family, ordination or the monastery of his first profession beyond 'the Cenobium' he says he left.

claims.claim: Envoys Hypatius, priest of Ephesus, and Demetrius came from Byzantium to the chief priest of Rome about a tenet of faith 'which is a subject of disagreement and controversy among the Christians'; 'although I know them well, I shall by no means make mention of them; for I consider it a sort of insane folly to investigate the nature of God'; God 'is altogether good and has all things in His power'
claims.witness: Procopius, Wars V.iii, tr. Dewing (wars-5-6 l.403-416)

claims.claim: Born late in the fifth century at Caesarea in Palestine; studied for the law; came young to Constantinople; in 527 legal adviser and private secretary to Belisarius; with him in Mesopotamia 527, Africa 533, Italy 536; an eyewitness
claims.witness: Dewing's introduction (wars-1-2 l.68-92)

claims.claim: 'It was at that time that Procopius, who wrote this history, was chosen as his adviser' (Belisarius made commander at Daras); the year 527 is Dewing's bracket
claims.witness: Procopius, Wars I.xiii (wars-1-2 l.1510-1512)

claims.claim: Belisarius, suspecting Silverius, chief priest of Rome, of treason with the Goths, sent him to Greece and appointed Vigilius
claims.witness: Procopius, Wars V.xxv (wars-5-6 l.3473-3476)

claims.claim: Hagia Sophia's dome 'does not appear to rest upon a solid foundation, but to cover the place beneath as though it were suspended from heaven by the fabled golden chain'
claims.witness: Procopius, Buildings I.i, tr. Stewart (l.493-496)

claims.claim: The History has a calm tone; the Buildings is 'written in the empty style of the fawning flatterer' yet 'a storehouse of information concerning the internal administration of the empire'
claims.witness: Dewing's introduction (wars-1-2 l.164, 181-191)

claims.claim: The Secret History attacks the emperor and empress and even Belisarius and Antonina; 'the very extravagance of the calumny makes it impossible to be believed'; 'very few contradictions in statements of fact'; not published until after Justinian's death in 565
claims.witness: Dewing's introduction (wars-1-2 l.141-160)

claims.claim: The Secret History 'on the whole gives a faithful picture of the Byzantine Court of the period', though details may be exaggerated
claims.witness: Athenian Society translator's preface (l.183-186)

claims.claim: The Secret History is Procopius's work
claims.witness: Dewing: 'now believed to be highly probable at least' (wars-1-2 l.162-170); the 1896 translator: 'Direct proofs of authenticity are wanting', the first to attribute it, Suidas and Nicephorus Callistus, 'lived centuries later' (l.155-158)

claims.claim: He writes 'at times as a Christian, and at times as one imbued with the ideas of the ancient religion of Greece'
claims.witness: Dewing's introduction (wars-1-2 l.205-211)

claims.claim: Of a sceptical turn of mind, indifferent, he 'affected the forms and language of Christianity' under an orthodox emperor; his writings do not decide the question
claims.witness: Athenian Society translator's preface (l.94-102)

claims.claim: Made senator and Prefect of Byzantium in 562; died shortly before or after 565
claims.witness: Athenian Society translator's preface (l.76-84); the Palestine Pilgrims' Text Society preface (Buildings l.96-110: 'is supposed to have died in 565')

claims.claim: His own activity continued till well nigh the end of Justinian's life
claims.witness: Dewing's introduction (wars-1-2 l.81-82)

contested_claims.sides: Dewing: he writes at times as a Christian and at times as one imbued with the old Greek religion, perhaps unconsciously from his study of the classics; it was politic to espouse the religion of the state (wars-1-2 l.205-211). The 1896 translator: a sceptic, indifferent, who affected Christian forms (l.94-102). Neither settles it; the translator says his writings do not.

contested_claims.claim: How far the Secret History can be believed
contested_claims.sides: Dewing: overdone, its calumny 'impossible to be believed', though with few contradictions in fact (wars-1-2 l.141-155). The 1896 translator: founded 'sometimes upon fact, sometimes upon vague rumours', but on the whole 'a faithful picture' (l.150-186).

absent_details.detail: The points of faith the envoys carried
absent_details.note: Procopius says he knew them and would not record them (Wars V.iii). The brief does not supply them.

absent_details.detail: His birth year and death year
absent_details.note: No held source gives a firm year. Dewing says late in the fifth century; the 1896 translator 'towards the beginning of the sixth century'; the Pilgrims' Text Society preface 'early in the sixth or at the end of the fifth century'. The death in or near 565 is given as supposed.

claims.claim: In the district called Tricurius he found men worshipping an idol with a play, an image on a hilltop; with two brothers he admonished them; the writer says he has been on that hill and traced with his hand the cross Samson carved with an iron instrument on a standing stone
claims.witness: Life I.48 (Taylor, samson-of-dol_life-of-st-samson_taylor1925.txt l.3874-3897)

claims.claim: Tricurius is the Hundred of Trigg in Cornwall
claims.witness: Taylor's note (Taylor, samson-of-dol_life-of-st-samson_taylor1925.txt l.3900)

claims.claim: His parents brought him as a boy to the school of Eltut, of all the Britons the most accomplished in the Scriptures and learning; at five, by Taylor's summary
claims.witness: Life I.7 (Taylor, samson-of-dol_life-of-st-samson_taylor1925.txt l.2339-2347); Taylor's sketch (l.455-457)

claims.claim: Career: Piro's monastery, abbot on Piro's death, a visit to Ireland, ordained bishop, Cornwall, Brittany, founded Dol, died and was buried there
claims.witness: Taylor's sketch from the Life (l.458-495); Life I.52, I.61 (l.4040-4048, 4286-4293)

claims.claim: He went to King Hiltbert on behalf of the captive Judual; Taylor identifies Hiltbert as Childebert
claims.witness: Life I.53-59 (l.4063-4074, 4250-4260); Taylor's introduction and index (l.609-611, 5373)

claims.claim: The Life tells miracles, among them the dove at his ordination as deacon and serpents driven out
claims.witness: Life (l.2595-2622, 3938-3960, 4262-4268); Taylor: the biographer accepted the miracles as authentic (l.497-502)

claims.claim: The writer wrote at the request of Bishop Tigernomalus, from what an old man, a cousin of Samson and a deacon, told him, and from accounts the deacon Henoc had brought
The writer is anonymous
claims.witness: Taylor ('our anonymous writer', l.537-538; 'The anonymous author', l.1615)

claims.claim: Duine found no trace of any literary composition later than the end of the sixth century; Taylor takes this as a convincing argument for 610-615
claims.witness: Taylor's introduction (l.725-743, 1651-1652)

claims.claim: Fawtier charged the author with untruthfulness, declared the work spurious, and did not accept its statements on authorship and provenance; Duine and Loth answered him
claims.witness: Taylor's introduction (l.567-575, 1652-1654)

claims.claim: Taylor reckons his consecration probably in 521 and his birth in 486, assuming he was then thirty-five
claims.witness: Taylor's sketch (l.448-455)

claims.claim: A Samson signed the council of Paris: 'Samson subscripsi et consensi in nomine Christi'; Maassen dates the council 556-573
claims.witness: Maassen, Concilia aevi Merovingici (concilia-aevi-merovingici-mgh-concilia-1-lat_maassen1893.txt l.11857; heading l.11525, 11838)

claims.claim: The signature names no see; Maassen's note gives 'Dolensis (?)' with Duchesne, and his index lists Samson as bishop of Dol
Taylor: Samson attended a council at Paris and signed among the bishops between 556 and 573
claims.witness: Taylor's introduction (l.1247-1250)

claims.claim: Later Lives rivalled this one's miracles; it 'actually furnished the mould into which many of them were cast'
claims.witness: Taylor's introduction (l.535-542)

claims.claim: A later Life of Illtud counts Samson, Paulinus, Gildas and Dewi among Illtud's pupils
claims.witness: Vita Iltuti, ed. Rees (rees_lives-of-the-cambro-british-saints-lat-eng_1853.txt l.7949-7951)

claims.claim: The Vita Samsonis cannot be earlier than the seventh century, because its writer knows the Homilies of Gregory I, nor later than Nominoe, that is 824
claims.witness: Hugh Williams, note in his edition of Gildas (gildas_de-excidio-britanniae-lorica-penitential-lat-eng_williams1899.txt l.18737-18740)

contested_claims.claim: When the Life of Samson was written, and whether its account of its sources is true
contested_claims.sides: Taylor (l.742-743, 1651-1652, 1708-1715), following Abbé Duine (l.725-731): 610-615, by a truthful writer. Fawtier, as Taylor reports him (l.567-575, 1652-1654): spurious, its statements on authorship and provenance rejected. Duine and Loth answered Fawtier (l.574-575). Fawtier's own date is not given in the held file. Hugh Williams, editing Gildas (gildas_de-excidio-britanniae-lorica-penitential-lat-eng_williams1899.txt l.18737-18740): no earlier than the seventh century, since the writer knows Gregory I's Homilies, and no later than Nominoe, that is 824.

absent_details.note: The Life gives none; Taylor gives none. The scan's 565 rests on no held line.
No writing of his own is held beyond the council signature.

absent_details.detail: Fawtier's own dating of the Life
absent_details.note: Taylor reports Fawtier's objections but not his date; Fawtier's book is not held.
